A statewide zoning-reform impact model

Hawaii doesn't have a housing shortage because people won't build. It has one because almost nothing pencils for who actually lives here.

What this is

This is a submission to the Housing Data and Technology Innovation Challenge: a statewide zoning-reform impact model for Hawaii. The Challenge asked teams to build a tool that measures how specific reforms — more units per lot, density near transit, smaller parking minimums — would actually change the housing supply, not just whether they're legally allowed.

So this tool keeps two questions separate at every step: what's legally buildable today (zoning capacity) versus what a specific reform would add on top of that (the policy's own incremental effect). A reform's total theoretical capacity is never reported as if it were the reform's impact — only the difference between baseline and reform counts.

Three reforms are modeled against real parcel, zoning, income, sales, and transit data: ADUs (accessory units on existing lots), Missing Middle (2–6 units per lot), and Transit-Oriented Density (upzoning near real bus/rail stops). A fourth, Parking Requirement Reduction, is modeled separately since it doesn't add units directly — it changes what else is feasible to build. Every parcel that clears a reform's zoning test is then run through a real development pro forma (does it pencil to build?) and an affordability gate (can the tract's own households actually afford it?) before counting toward any headline number.

How to read the other tabs

  • Existing Conditions — the starting point: how much is already zoned and buildable right now, county by county and tract by tract, independent of any reform.
  • Scenario Explorer — pick one or more counties and reforms and see the incremental units each would add, on the map and in headline totals.
  • Assumptions & Methodology — where every number in this tool comes from: the formulas, the real market data behind them, and the sourced constants (construction costs, mortgage rates, absorption rates) that feed the pro forma.

Scenario shown on the map

View

Feasibility asks whether a developer could profitably build and sell/rent at the comps-implied price. Affordability-constrained asks a different question: of THAT price, what share of the tract's own households could actually afford it (20% down, 7.000% 30-yr fixed — HiCentral, 30% of income — against real ACS household-income brackets, not a median guess)? A tract can be feasible to build and still be unaffordable to nearly everyone who lives there.

Absorption rate

Share of zoned capacity assumed to actually get built over the model's 10-year horizon. Defaults to each scenario's own county benchmark; drag to test sensitivity.

Transit mode

HB1409 (2025)/Act 159, HRS §206E-246(j): FAR 4.0 within ½ mile of ANY real transit station (mode-agnostic by the statute's own text). The higher 6.0/7.0 tiers apply only near a station on an adopted "locally preferred alternative" (LPA) project — in Hawaii today, that's HART's Skyline rail and nothing else, so Rail mode reaches those tiers and Bus mode is capped at 4.0 regardless of distance. FAR is now the real per-parcel tier computed from actual distance to the nearest stop, not a slider.

Development fee reduction

$0 (full waiver)$50,000$75,000

Savings flow dollar-for-dollar into the feasibility pro forma's excess value. $50,000 is the Challenge's standardized baseline fee (toggle off = this, unchanged); the $0–$75,000 range is bounded by Honolulu DPP's own published per-unit fee stack — wastewater ($6,616) + water ($4,200–8,000) + building permit (~$2,200) + park dedication-in-lieu ($24,000–57,000), ≈$37,000– 74,000 combined — not left open-ended. No published Kauai-specific fee schedule was found; this is the best available statewide bound. See Model & Assumptions.

Totals, selected counties

Units this policy enables: 0. Parking Requirement Reduction does not change eligibility or unit count on Kauai — ADUs already require only 1 space either way under current code, so removing that requirement doesn't unlock any new unit count in this model. This matches what Sohoni & Lee's 2025 study of nine U.S. cities that removed parking minimums would predict for a place like Kauai: a real lever, but a minimal-effect one outside dense urban markets. The chart below is showing something different — land freed up by removing the requirement (sqft, not units), which only really matters on parcels large enough for bigger development; see Model & Assumptions for the full methodology.
Transit-Oriented Density applies HB1409 (2025)/Act 159's enacted FAR-based "transit-supportive density" standard (HRS §206E-246(j)/226-63(d)) using the SAME mechanism for every county and mode: FAR is the real statutory tier based on each parcel's actual distance to its nearest transit stop of the selected mode, not a slider. Bus stops (TheBus/Kauai Bus, real GTFS data) are capped at the statute's FAR 4.0 base tier within ½ mile — real transit stations, but not an adopted "locally preferred alternative" (LPA) project. Rail (HART Skyline, Honolulu only) is the one LPA project in Hawaii today, so it reaches FAR 6.0 within ½ mile and FAR 7.0 within ¼ mile. Even the base FAR of 4.0, applied across every parcel within ½ mile of a bus stop in a dense network, produces a very large total — real Hawaii TOD programs apply these FAR tiers to small, specifically-designated station-area overlays, not every bus-served block; this dashboard shows the number the statute's own text implies anyway, rather than hiding it. Feasibility now tests BOTH a for-sale and a rental product for every parcel and takes whichever pencils better (added 2026-10-15, next day's work) — not "either feasible, so built," which would double-count the same capacity under both tenures. The rental side comes from the State of Hawaii OPSD Skyline TOD Feasibility Study's real market-rate rental inputs ($3,200/mo rent, 4.5% cap rate, $574,080/unit stabilized value), scaled by each tract's own real ACS median gross rent; no rental developer-profit margin is subtracted, since none is sourced anywhere in the study — a real, stated gap that makes the rental side a more permissive bar than the for-sale side. Each tract's affordability-constrained units are then checked against the income distribution matching whichever tenure won that tract — real owner-household brackets (ACS B19001) or real renter-household brackets (ACS B25118) — so the dashboard can report how much of a reform's impact would create owner-occupied vs. rental housing, not one blended number. See Model & Assumptions for the full methodology, the before/after figures by reform, and its stated limitations.

How much of a reform's capacity actually gets built, in a given decade

The absorption-rate slider's default isn't a round guess — it's each county's own historical building-permit activity as a share of its housing stock. The blended bar is what the slider defaults to (a multi-year FRED average, smoothing over COVID); the pre-COVID bar isolates 2019 alone from the newly-added Census Building Permits Survey monthly export, the one full year before the 2020 permitting disruption.

Grounds: `absorption_rate_benchmark_for()` reads the blended figure as the slider's default for every reform's raw-capacity-to-estimated-units step; the pre-COVID figure is shown here for comparison, not yet used as a default itself — Kaua'i and Honolulu move in opposite directions between the two, which is the actual reason to look at both rather than trusting one blended number. See building_permits_by_type.csv for the full 2019–2025 county-by-structure-type panel this is built from.

Zoned capacity = units already built + whatever legal headroom today's zoning allows beyond that, with no reform. Headroom is two enacted, already-in-force rules combined: the Missing Middle density-per-acre headroom (Kaua'i only — Honolulu's piece of this is 0, a real, stated data gap, no sourced density-per-acre rule for Honolulu's R-districts yet, not a finding that no headroom exists) and Act 39/SB3202's statewide 2-ADU-per-lot mandate (both counties — current law, not a reform, same figure the Scenario Explorer's ADU default already uses as its baseline). See the Methodology tab's ADU and Missing Middle sections for exactly how each is computed.

Enacted law tells this model what to simulate; failed bills tell it how to design the next one

Hawaii's own legislative record does two different jobs here. A statute that's already law is a direct input — its own language becomes the scenario's zoning-capacity rule, as-is, not a guess at what reform might look like. A bill that didn't pass is a design signal instead — it shows where a future state-level reform stalls, and what a version built to actually clear committee would need to do differently.

Every number on this page's other two tabs comes from a formula below, not a guess — this page exists so anyone can check the math. For each reform: what it does to the housing numbers, what assumptions went in, where those assumptions came from, and the actual formula. The full narrative write-ups (including every dead end and correction along the way) live in Model & Assumptions Overview, Data Provenance, and Existing Conditions.

Baseline vs. policy intervention — the rule every reform below follows

Every scenario answers one question: what does a reform add on top of current law, not what a parcel's total theoretical capacity is. A parcel's current-code capacity (what it can already legally hold today) is computed first and subtracted off; only the capacity a reform adds beyond that baseline is ever reported as the reform's impact. This single rule is applied identically in all four reforms below — it's why each one's formula includes an existing_units_estimate or baseline_capacity subtraction term.

The baseline itself is now also directly reported, not just subtracted off (added 2026-10-16): ADU's own number below already is the baseline scenario — current law's 2-ADU-per-lot mandate, not a reform (the premise its own section states). Missing Middle's baseline — what today's zoning already allows beyond what's built, with no reform at all — is now reported as its own figure in that section below, not just used internally to decide which parcels the reform touches. TOD's baseline was a real gap until this pass: it previously netted its reform capacity against only what's physically built today, not what current zoning already allows; it now nets out whichever is larger, so a parcel's own unused legal headroom under today's law is never miscredited to the TOD reform.

ADU (Accessory Dwelling Units)

What it does: models Act 39/SB3202's real, already-enacted mandate — at least 2 ADUs per residentially-zoned lot — against Kauai's actual current density code, to find which parcels can legally add a second unit today.

Assumptions: eligibility requires (1) a single-family-zoned (R-numbered) parcel, (2) an existing residential unit on it, and (3) the district's real units/acre allowance covering existing_units_estimate + 1 on that parcel's actual area. No owner-occupancy requirement is assumed (Kauai's code has none, confirmed directly against the ordinance text) and no parking constraint gates eligibility (see Parking Requirement Reduction below for why). existing_units_estimate assumes 1 unit per already-residential parcel — Kauai has no direct unit-count field, so this is a stated simplification, not a measured count.

Sources: Kauai County Code §8-4.2(b)/§8-4.6 (the real per-district units/acre density rule, confirmed against the ordinance text, not inferred from zoning labels); Act 39 (2024)/SB3202 (see the Existing Conditions legislation section above).

Formula:

eligible = zone_is_R_district AND has_existing_residential_unit
           AND (max_units_by_density >= existing_units_estimate + 1)
estimated_new_units_per_tract = count(eligible_parcels_in_tract) × absorption_rate

Impact on the numbers: 2,297 eligible parcels countywide → 144.7 raw estimated units at the 6.3% absorption-rate default → 108.2 feasibility-adjusted units (3 of 17 tracts fail feasibility entirely) → 0 affordability-constrained units (every Kauai household earns below the required income for the comps-implied price in every tract — see the Affordability-Constrained Demand Gate below).

Kauai's current zoning already allows ~1,923 more units than are built — before any reform

That's the baseline: capacity under today's law, not a Missing Middle intervention. The reform below only touches parcels current zoning does NOT already permit this on.

Missing Middle (2–6 units)

What it does: models upzoning to the Challenge's own 2–6-unit benchmark ceiling, but only on parcels current density code restricts to exactly their existing unit count (the same single-family-restricted parcels the ADU scenario would otherwise also touch).

Assumptions: a parcel the district's density math already lets build past its current unit count (most larger R-6+ lots) is excluded — that's already-legal baseline capacity, not a reform effect, and counting it here would double-count it as "impact." AG/O/C-N/C-G parcels are excluded entirely (no units/acre figure exists to compute against). Buildable-area check, added 2026-10-15: a parcel's reform capacity is also capped at floor(parcel_area_sqft / 815 sqft) — 815 sqft is RentCafe/Yardi Matrix's real blended average unit size for Oahu apartment buildings with 50+ units, replacing a for-sale-townhome figure this project previously had no better option than borrowing. This check is single-story-equivalent (no credit for the Challenge's own "up to 3 stories" allowance), so it's a conservative floor-area cap, not a precise one — stated rather than inventing a stories/coverage multiplier with no cited source. Not summed with the ADU scenario for the same parcel, since both draw on the same underlying density allowance — a combined number would need to take the max of the two, not their sum (not yet wired in).

Sources: same density ordinance as ADU (Kauai County Code §8-4.2(b)/§8-4.6); the 2–6-unit/3-story ceiling is the Challenge benchmark's own stated definition of "Missing Middle," not a Kauai-specific figure; RentCafe/Yardi Matrix's Oahu apartment market page (rentcafe.com/average-rent-market-trends/us/hi/oahu/) for the 815 sqft unit-size figure.

Formula:

eligible = baseline_capacity == 0   (currently single-family-restricted in practice)
reform_capacity_cap = min(6, floor(parcel_area_sqft / 815))
additional_unit_capacity = max(0, reform_capacity_cap − existing_units_estimate)   [for eligible parcels only]
additional_estimated_units_per_tract = sum(additional_unit_capacity_in_tract) × absorption_rate

Impact on the numbers: 4,095.5 raw estimated units countywide at the absorption-rate default (down slightly from 4,163.8 before the buildable-area check, since it only binds on Kauai's smallest lots) → 2,899.1 feasibility-adjusted units (29% gated out by the same per-tract feasible/infeasible pattern as ADU) → 0 affordability-constrained units, for the same reason as ADU: the for-sale product's comps-implied price clears no Kauai household's real income in any tract.

Baseline scenario (added 2026-10-16, per direct request): the number above is the REFORM's incremental impact. Separately, Kauai's existing zoning — with no reform at all — already permits an estimated 1,922.8 units (30,521 gross units of legal headroom across 3,160 parcels, scaled by the same absorption rate) beyond what's currently built: real R-20+ lots whose density math already allows more density than exists today. This was computed internally since the Missing Middle buildable-area work (as the == 0 eligibility filter that decides which parcels the reform even applies to) but never itself reported until now — see `run_missing_middle_baseline_tract()` in Model & Assumptions. Honolulu's equivalent baseline is 0 everywhere — a real, stated data gap (no sourced density-per-acre rule for Honolulu's R-districts), not a finding that no headroom exists there.

Transit-Oriented Density (TOD)

What it does: models the real, enacted floor-area-ratio (FAR) density standard from HB1409 (2024)/Act 159, HRS §206E-246(j) and the TOD-area definition it incorporates from HRS §226-63(d) — a statute that is itself mode-agnostic (it never says "rail" or "bus," only "transit hub or transit station"). Rebuilt 2026-10-15 to use ONE mechanism for every county and mode, replacing two different ad hoc per-county buffer tests: tod_eligible_parcels (county, mode) computes each parcel's real distance to the nearest GTFS-derived transit stop of the selected mode and assigns the statute's own FAR tier directly from that distance — no buffer-boolean test, no user-set FAR slider.

Assumptions: FAR 4.0 (the statute's base tier) applies within ½ mile of any real transit stop, bus or rail — that is what §226-63(d) means by a "county-designated TOD area" absent the county's own designation. The higher 6.0/7.0 (½ mile / ¼ mile) tiers apply only near a station of an adopted "locally preferred alternative" (LPA) mass-transit project — in Hawaii today, that is HART's Skyline rail and nothing else, so bus mode (TheBus/Kauai Bus) is capped at the 4.0 base tier everywhere, while rail mode (HART Skyline, Honolulu only) can reach 6.0/7.0 near its 13 open stations. Unit size is 815 GSF — RentCafe/Yardi Matrix's real blended average unit size for Oahu apartment buildings with 50+ units (pulled 2026-10-15), replacing a townhome-based for-sale figure this project previously borrowed for lack of a better option: a townhome isn't a comparable product to a TOD or Missing Middle apartment unit. No comparable 50+-unit survey exists for Kauai, so the same Oahu-sourced figure is applied to both counties, stated rather than hidden. Unlike ADU/Missing Middle, non-R zones (AG/O/C-N/C-G) are NOT excluded — the statute applies "for all uses permitted ... under underlying county zoning."

Sources: HB1409 (2024)/Act 159 (enacted, in force — legiscan.com/HI/text/HB1409/ id/3222589), HRS §206E-246(j) and §226-63(d) (data.capitol.hawaii.gov) for the FAR tiers and TOD-area definition; the real combined GTFS feed for Honolulu (MobilityDatabase mdb-2350, producer thebus.org — carries both TheBus and HART Skyline rail in one feed, agency_id "Skyline"/route_id "181") and Kauai Bus's own GTFS feed (NTD ID 90237) for stop/route data; RentCafe/Yardi Matrix's Oahu apartment market page (rentcafe.com/average-rent-market-trends/us/hi/oahu/) for the 815 sqft unit-size figure. SB1614, the TOD companion bill, did not pass (died in committee, carried over with an effective date set to 2050) and is not relied on for anything here.

Formula:

tod_far = statutory tier by real distance to nearest GTFS stop of the selected mode
          (4.0 within ½mi of any stop; 6.0/7.0 within ½mi/¼mi only if mode is an LPA project)
reform_capacity = floor(parcel_area_sqft × tod_far / 815)
true_baseline = max(existing_units_estimate, max_units_by_density)   (built units, or current zoning's own
                                                                        legal headroom, whichever is larger)
additional_capacity = max(0, reform_capacity − true_baseline)   [tod_eligible parcels only]
additional_estimated_units_per_tract = sum(additional_capacity_in_tract) × absorption_rate

Baseline fix (added 2026-10-16, per direct request): this used to subtract only existing_units_estimate — what's physically built today — which overstated TOD's reform impact on any parcel whose CURRENT (non-TOD) zoning already permits more units than exist, since that unused legal headroom is baseline capacity under today's law, not something the TOD FAR bonus unlocks. Now nets out whichever is larger: what's built, or what today's zoning already allows (`max_units_by_density` — the same field Missing Middle's own baseline uses, above). For Kauai the effect is small (most eligible parcels have little such headroom); for Honolulu it has no effect at all, since the same missing density-per-acre data behind Missing Middle's 0 baseline there means this field is 0 for every Honolulu parcel too — stated, not hidden.

Impact on the numbers — an honest, unresolved finding: applying even the base FAR of 4.0 to every parcel within ½ mile of a bus stop in a dense network produces a very large total — real Hawaii TOD programs apply these FAR tiers to small, specifically-designated station-area overlays, not every bus-served block. The dashboard shows this deliberately unresolved rather than narrowing the eligibility footprint without a cited basis for doing so — the real suspected problem is the footprint's breadth, not the density figure itself. See Model & Assumptions for current figures by county and mode.

Feasibility and affordability (added 2026-10-15, next day's work): TOD is a rental apartment product, not the for-sale townhome ADU/Missing Middle/Parking Reduction test, so it now runs through its own gate, tract_scaled_rental_feasibility(county). Revenue comes from the State of Hawaii OPSD Skyline TOD Feasibility Study's real market-rate rental inputs ($3,200/mo rent, 2.5% vacancy, 40% opex, 4.5% cap rate, $574,080/unit stabilized value), re-fetched and re-confirmed to contain no rental developer-profit margin anywhere in the document — the for-sale product's 15% margin is explicitly a for-sale figure and was never transferable, so none is subtracted here, a stated gap that makes this a more permissive bar than the for-sale gates. The 4.5% cap rate is cross-checked against the study's own real Study Area figure (4.4%) and a second, independent but weakly-sourced source (apartmentloanstore.com, Class A multifamily 4.70%) — both corroborate the order of magnitude. Revenue is scaled by each tract's own real ACS median gross rent relative to the countywide figure, not home value; costs reuse each county's already-sourced for-sale hard/land cost figures. The affordability gate tests against the real ACS B25118 renter-occupied-household income distribution, not the blended all-household one used elsewhere. Result: 9 of 31 Honolulu rail-eligible tracts with rental data now clear feasibility, versus 0 of 34 under the old (mismatched) for-sale gate. See Model & Assumptions and Data Sources for full figures and sourcing.

Parking Requirement Reduction

What it does to the housing numbers: nothing, directly. Parking does not gate ADU eligibility on Kauai — a parcel either qualifies for a second unit under the density rule above or it doesn't, and current code already requires only 1 off-street space per ADU either way. Removing that requirement doesn't make any additional parcel eligible, so this scenario reports the same eligible-parcel count as the ADU scenario (2,297), not a unit-count change. What actually changes is land freed on each eligible parcel that the parking requirement would otherwise consume.

Assumptions: 200 sqft/space (a standard surface-parking stall + maneuvering allowance) — a planning-literature figure, not Kauai-specific, the same evidentiary status as other inherited planning benchmarks in this model. This project deliberately does NOT apply a quantitative post-reform parking-supply reduction ratio to Kauai: Sohoni & Lee (2025) found parking reform's effect ranges from minimal (Grand Rapids, Hartford) to large (Champaign, Somerville) depending on a city's density and car-dependency — and Kauai's own real ACS figures (~5% non-car commute share, ~675 people/sq mi) sit below even the study's "minimal effect" anchor cities on both axes, meaning a numeric reduction ratio would be extrapolation past the regression's support, not interpolation within it.

Sources: Kauai County Code Chapter 8, Article 15/§8-1.4(i) (the real confirmed 1-space/ADU requirement); Sohoni & Lee, "Parking the Minimum Parking Requirement: Evidence from Nine U.S. Cities," Journal of Planning Education and Research 46(1), 2025 (doi.org/10.1177/0739456X251343047) — Table 3's real before/after parking-supply figures for 9 cities, used for the density/car-dependency comparison, not for a reduction ratio applied to Kauai; ACS 2022 5-year commute/density data for Kauai's own position on those same two axes.

Formula:

eligible_parcels = (same set as the ADU scenario -- unchanged by this reform)
parking_land_consumed_sqft_per_tract = count(eligible_parcels_in_tract) × 200

Impact on the numbers: 2,297 eligible parcels × 200 sqft/space = 459,400 sqft (10.5 acres) of parking land freed countywide if the requirement is eliminated — real, but modest at the scale of the county's 4,914-unit shortage, and zero additional units this model can attribute to the reform directly. This is why the Scenario Explorer labels this chart "Land freed, sqft (NOT units)" rather than a units column.

Development Fee Reduction & the feasibility gate

What it does: answers whether a parcel's zoning capacity is actually profitable to build, using a real Kauai-specific development pro forma — not just whether it's legal. This is the gate that converts every reform's "zoning capacity" into its "feasibility-adjusted" number above.

Assumptions: uses the "excess value" test (market value − total development cost − required developer profit ≥ 0) from a real Kaua'i-specific pro forma (Lihu'e Town Core submarket), not an invented cost structure. Land cost is allocated as $/building-GSF (the source table's land price per sqft of residential building area), not a true site-area/FAR-based allocation — a stated simplification, since no per-district FAR/land-value data exists for Kauai yet. Financing cost uses an average-outstanding-balance approximation (loan amount × rate × term × 0.5, plus origination fees), not a full monthly draw schedule. The reference sale price is scaled to each tract's own ACS median home value (a linear heuristic: a tract twice as expensive as the county median is assumed to sell new product at roughly twice the reference price) — cost inputs stay fixed at the Lihu'e table's figures everywhere, since no tract-level cost data exists.

Sources: State of Hawaii OPSD, "Financial Analysis of TOD Infrastructure Funding and Financing Options" (HR&A Advisors et al., 2023) — Real Estate Assumptions table, Lihu'e Town Core (Kaua'i) column, sourced in the original to Group Pacific/PBR Hawai'i (hard costs), HR&A (soft costs, developer profit), CBRE (financing terms), and CoStar/Zillow (sale prices); the Challenge's own mandated $50,000/unit standardized development fee; Honolulu DPP's Affordable Housing Requirement Incentives handout (Feb. 2025) for the real $37,000–$74,000 fee-component stack bounding the slider's range; ACS 2022 5-year median home value (B25077) for the tract-scaling denominator.

Formula:

hard_cost = unit_size_gsf × hard_cost_per_gsf        ($420/GSF townhome, 1,500 GSF → $630,000)
soft_cost = hard_cost × 0.15
land_cost = unit_size_gsf × $36/building-GSF
loan_amount = (hard_cost + soft_cost + land_cost) × 0.60   (60% loan-to-cost)
financing_cost = loan_amount × 7.0% × 2yrs × 0.5 + loan_amount × 2.5% (fees)
total_development_cost = hard + soft + land + financing + development_fee
sale_price = reference_price × (tract_median_home_value / countywide_median_home_value)
required_developer_profit = sale_price × 15%
excess_value = sale_price − total_development_cost − required_developer_profit
feasible = (excess_value ≥ 0)

Impact on the numbers: at the Challenge's $50,000 standardized fee, the Lihu'e reference townhome's excess_value is positive countywide, but 3 of 17 tracts (the below-median-home-value ones, where the scaled sale price can't clear this fixed cost structure) come back infeasible — the source of ADU's 108.2→ the same 108.2 figure (no tracts newly flip) and Missing Middle's 29% cut. A fee change (the fee-reduction slider) moves excess_value dollar-for-dollar: at the real Honolulu-sourced $37,000–$74,000 fee-component range, the maximum possible swing is too small to flip any of those 3 infeasible tracts to feasible — the "fee reduction alone won't close the gap" finding documented in the Scenario Explorer's own fee-reduction note.

Update (2026-10-15, next day's work): this for-sale test no longer runs alone — ADU and Missing Middle (like TOD) now also run a rental pro forma on the same tracts and the model takes whichever one pencils better, tagging which tenure "won." This is what lets the dashboard report, e.g., how many of ADU's feasibility-adjusted units would plausibly be built (and bought) as owner-occupied housing versus built (and rented) as rental housing. See the TOD section's note above and Model & Assumptions for the dual-tenure mechanism and the real for-sale/rental split by reform.

Affordability-constrained demand gate

What it does: a demand-side question distinct from feasibility — of the comps-implied price a feasible project would charge, what share of a tract's own households could actually afford it? A tract can clear feasibility (a developer's return pencils at the going price) while still being a market of a handful of local households who could ever pay that price — this gate is how the dashboard catches that, rather than reporting feasibility alone as the finish line.

Assumptions: standard mortgage underwriting — 20% down, 30-year fixed, monthly principal+interest capped at 30% of gross income (the HUD/Census "cost-burdened" standard, not a project-invented threshold). Principal + interest ONLY — excludes property tax, homeowner's insurance, and HOA/CPR fees (common on Kauai condo/CPR units), since no Hawaii-specific property-tax-rate or insurance-cost source is in this project yet. This means required income is an UNDERSTATEMENT of the true bar — the real qualifying percentage is at or below what this model computes, never above it. Treats "% of tract households who could afford the unit" as a direct ceiling on units absorbed in that tract specifically — a conservative, locally-grounded assumption that undercounts regional demand (buyers from a wider commute-shed aren't counted), not a claim that every qualifying household is in the market this year (that's what the separate absorption rate is for — the two stack multiplicatively, not interchangeably).

Sources: Census ACS 5-year detailed table B19001 (Household Income in the Past 12 Months), tract-level, 16 real income brackets — not a tract median used as a stand-in; HiCentral (Honolulu Board of REALTORS) real mortgage rate quotes (hicentral.com/hawaii-mortgage-rates.php, confirmed 2026-10-15) — median of 8 Hawaii-market lenders' 30-yr fixed rate, 7.000%, excluding one non-Hawaii-market outlier. This section covers the for-sale product (ADU/Missing Middle); TOD's rental affordability gate is separate and tests against ACS B25118's real renter-occupied-household income brackets, not B19001 — see the TOD section above.

Formula:

loan_amount = sale_price × (1 − 20%)
monthly_rate = 7.000% / 12;  n = 360 months
monthly_PI = loan_amount × [monthly_rate × (1+monthly_rate)^n] / [(1+monthly_rate)^n − 1]
required_income = (monthly_PI × 12) / 30%
pct_households_affording = share of the tract's real B19001 brackets with income ≥ required_income
                            (linear interpolation within whichever bracket the threshold falls inside)
affordability_adjusted_units = feasibility_adjusted_units × (pct_households_affording / 100)

Impact on the numbers — the headline finding: 0% of Kauai households clear the required-income bar in every single tract for the ADU/Missing Middle for-sale product — 108.2 feasibility-adjusted ADU units and 2,899.1 Missing Middle units both collapse to 0 affordability-constrained units countywide. The tracts where a project is feasible to build (high enough comps to cover cost + profit) are disproportionately Kauai's expensive tracts (Princeville/Hanalei North Shore) — $1.9M+ required sale prices, $400K+ required household income, which essentially no Kauai household has; the lower-priced tracts fail feasibility in the first place. There is essentially no overlap between "a developer could profitably build this" and "a Kauai household could afford to buy it," as currently modeled. The Existing Conditions "Household income & the affordability gap" chart is this same math run in the other direction, against the real sales comps directly.

Update (2026-10-15, next day's work): this is now specifically the result for whichever tracts the for-sale pro forma wins on feasibility (12 of Kauai's 17 tracts; 38 of Honolulu's 288). Tracts where the rental pro forma wins instead route through the real ACS B25118 renter-household income distribution, not this one — and that's where almost all of this project's real, nonzero affordability finding comes from (Kauai: 5.3 of 108.2 ADU units, 32.8 of 2,899.1 Missing Middle units; Honolulu's split is a genuine mix of both tenures). See Model & Assumptions for the full dual-tenure mechanism and figures by reform.

Absorption rate — how much of a reform's capacity actually gets built

What it does: every reform's zoning capacity is scaled by this single rate before feasibility/affordability are even applied — it's the model's stand-in for "not every legally eligible parcel redevelops in a given decade."

Assumptions: Kauai's default is 6.3% (not a round guess) — derived from each area's average annual permit count as a share of its housing stock, scaled to a 10-year horizon. This is NOT the same quantity a prior build's 8% assumption approximated (no historical eligible-parcel baseline exists for Hawaii either); it's the best available empirical proxy, not a measured redevelopment rate for ADU/Missing-Middle-eligible parcels specifically. Exposed as a UI slider so this uncertainty is adjustable, not hidden behind a fixed number.

Sources: FRED Building Permits Survey (series BPPRIV015001/3/7/9, HIBPPRIV) × Hawaii DBEDT 2023 housing-unit estimates (CO-EST2023-HU-15) — full figures in data/reference/absorption_rate_benchmarks.csv.

Formula:

absorption_rate = (avg_annual_building_permits / existing_housing_stock) × 10 years

Geography: tract vs. place

Hawaii has no incorporated cities — the entire state outside county government is unincorporated — so "place" in this tool means Census Designated Place (CDP), the only real place-name geography TIGERweb publishes for Hawaii. Each tract is assigned to whichever CDP covers the largest share of its land area (a real GIS spatial join, not a centroid guess or a name lookup); tracts with under 10% overlap with any CDP are labeled "Rural Kaua'i (unincorporated)" rather than force-assigned to a place they barely touch. When rolling tracts up to places, counts and land area are summed; rates and medians (rent, price/sqft, density) are weighted by the relevant denominator (households, sales count, population) — never a naive average of per-tract numbers, which would overweight a 3-household tract as much as a 900-household one. The Leaflet map itself stays at tract resolution regardless of the toggle.

Known limitations

  • Kauai only, so far — Oahu, Maui, and Hawai'i County are scaffolded in the UI but have no real data yet.
  • The affordability gate's mortgage calculation is principal-and-interest only — it excludes property tax, insurance, and HOA/CPR fees, so the true required income is understated, not overstated.
  • Feasibility's revenue side scales comps-implied price one-sidedly; it is a stated simplification, not a full market-clearing model.
  • Zillow publishes no ZIP-level rent data for Kauai — only one countywide ZORI figure exists, so the rent chart necessarily mixes tract-level ACS medians with a single countywide line.
  • The "over time" sales trend is 17 real months (Feb 2025–Jun 2026) — real transactions, but still shorter than ZORI's own 2015+ history.
  • The TOD scenario's eligibility footprint (over half the county) produces an implausible unit count at every density mechanism tried so far — presented deliberately unresolved, not papered over.
  • The 6.3% absorption rate is a statewide permit-to-stock proxy, not a measured redevelopment rate for reform-eligible parcels specifically.

Full detail: Model & Assumptions Overview §Limitations and Known Edge Cases.

Data: Kauai County parcels & zoning (State of Hawaii GIS), Census ACS 2022 5-year (commute mode, density, median home value), State TOD/development-cost figures from the State of Hawaii OPSD's Financial Analysis of TOD Infrastructure Funding and Financing Options (HR&A Advisors et al., 2023). Full methodology, data sources, and every stated assumption/simplification: see docs/MODEL_AND_ASSUMPTIONS.md and data/DATA_SOURCES.md in this repository. Generated from scripts/build_model.py — not updated automatically; regenerate the embedded data in data/sample/kauai_dashboard.geojson after a model change.
